steps.title: Baskets on the ground
steps.body: On Santorini, vines are trained into low baskets, called kouloura, woven from their own canes, lying on the ground. The grapes grow inside the basket. Each year the basket grows; after decades, growers cut it back and start again from the old roots. It's one of the oldest training systems in the world.

steps.title: Why baskets
steps.body: The kouloura protects grapes from Santorini's strong winds, which can reach over 50 km/h, and from fierce sun and sand. Inside, the grapes catch night humidity from sea mist, the vines' main water source. The low shape keeps the vines close to the ground, where it's cooler and more humid.

steps.prompt: What does the kouloura protect against?
steps.explanation: Santorini has mild winters; frost isn't the main concern.

steps.title: Tiny yields
steps.body: Santorini's yields are among the lowest in Europe, often 10 to 20 hectolitres per hectare, compared with 50 or more elsewhere. Old roots, drought and wind keep them low. Combined with steep land prices from tourism, this makes Santorini expensive and its vineyards endangered.

options: A basket-shaped vine trained on the ground
steps.explanation: Vines woven into baskets protect the fruit.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Kouloura vines are woven into baskets on the ground
They protect grapes from wind, sun and sand
Yields are tiny, among Europe's lowest
